nikolaus-ii#text: Nicholas II ascended the throne in 1894 and held fast to the principle of unlimited autocracy. Industry grew under him, but defeat by Japan in 1905 and Bloody Sunday sparked a revolution that forced him to issue the October Manifesto and allow a Duma. His family placed its hopes in the wandering holy man Grigory Rasputin because he seemed to ease the haemophilia of the heir to the throne, Alexei. In the First World War Nicholas took over supreme command himself in 1915 and was blamed for the defeats. After the February Revolution he abdicated in March 1917; in July 1918 Bolsheviks shot him and his family in Yekaterinburg.
jayavarman-ii#role: Founder of the Khmer Empire of Angkor
jayavarman-ii#summary: The king who united the Khmer and had himself consecrated as universal monarch on Phnom Kulen in 802.
jayavarman-ii#text: What we know of Jayavarman II comes mainly from an inscription written some 250 years after his time. According to it, he returned from "Java", subdued the Khmer principalities in long struggles and in 802 was consecrated as chakravartin on Mount Kulen. With this he renounced a foreign overlordship and founded a royal cult that accompanied the rulers of Angkor for centuries. He resided in several places, last at Hariharalaya near the Tonle Sap lake. His dates are uncertain; 835 or 850 are given as the year of his death.
ngo-quyen#role: General and first king of independent Vietnam
ngo-quyen#summary: The general who defeated the Chinese fleet on the Bạch Đằng River in 938 and thereby established Vietnam's independence.
ngo-quyen#text: Ngô Quyền was a military commander in the Red River Delta, which was then under Chinese rule. When the Southern Han kingdom sent a fleet in 938, he had iron-tipped stakes planted in the mouth of the Bạch Đằng and used the tides to destroy the enemy ships. In 939 he made himself king and chose the old citadel of Cổ Loa as his capital. After his death in 944 the country broke up for some years under the rule of local lords. In Vietnam he is still regarded as a national hero.
anawrahta#summary: The king who from 1044 created the first kingdom in present-day Myanmar and promoted Theravada Buddhism.
anawrahta#text: Anawrahta ruled at Pagan from 1044 and extended his power through campaigns over large parts of the Irrawaddy valley. According to tradition he conquered the Mon city of Thaton in 1057 and brought monks and texts of Theravada Buddhism to Pagan, supported by the monk Shin Arahan. He had irrigation works near Kyaukse expanded, securing the rice supply, and began building the Shwezigon Pagoda. His dates follow the Burmese chronicles and are not entirely certain. In Myanmar he is regarded as the founder of the nation.
jayavarman-vii#summary: The Buddhist Khmer king who built Angkor Thom and the Bayon and under whom the empire reached its greatest extent.
jayavarman-vii#text: Jayavarman VII freed Angkor from the Cham, who had sacked the city in 1177, and was crowned in 1181. He was a Mahayana Buddhist and built more than any other Khmer king: the city of Angkor Thom with the Bayon, the temple monasteries of Ta Prohm and Preah Khan, and hospitals and rest houses along the roads. His campaigns brought Champa under Khmer rule for a time. Some scholars see in the faces of the Bayon his likeness or that of a bodhisattva. After his death around 1218 later rulers had many Buddhist images removed again.
ramkhamhaeng#summary: The king of Sukhothai who is revered in Thailand as the creator of the Thai script and the model of a just ruler.
ramkhamhaeng#text: Ramkhamhaeng reigned from about 1279 and extended Sukhothai's influence far to the south and west. He promoted Theravada Buddhism and sent embassies to China. The famous inscription of 1292, found in 1833 by the future King Mongkut, portrays him as a fatherly king to whom any subject could come with a request, and attributes the Thai script to him. Since the 1980s some scholars have doubted that the inscription really dates from his time. His year of birth is unknown, and the year of his death is not certain either.
gajah-mada#role: Chief minister of the kingdom of Majapahit
gajah-mada#summary: The powerful minister under whom Majapahit rose to become the leading power of the Indonesian archipelago in the 14th century.
gajah-mada#text: Gajah Mada rose from officer of the royal guard to patih, chief minister of Majapahit. According to Javanese tradition he swore the Palapa oath, renouncing worldly pleasures until the archipelago was united under Majapahit. Under him and King Hayam Wuruk the kingdom extended its influence to Bali, Sumatra, Borneo and the east of the archipelago. In 1357 an attempt to arrange a marriage with a princess from West Java ended in a bloody clash that weakened his influence. In today's Indonesia he is a symbol of national unity; his year of birth and origins are unknown.
parameswara#role: Founder and first ruler of Malacca
parameswara#summary: The prince from Palembang who founded Malacca around 1400 and placed it under the protection of the Ming dynasty.
parameswara#text: Parameswara came from the princely house of Palembang on Sumatra, which claimed the heritage of Srivijaya. After conflicts with Majapahit he fled to Temasek, today's Singapore, and around 1400 founded Malacca on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula. He sought China's protection against Siam and Majapahit, received the fleets of Zheng He and in 1411 travelled in person to the court of the Yongle Emperor. Whether he himself converted to Islam is disputed among scholars; his successors at the latest were Muslims. His dates are known only approximately.
afonso-de-albuquerque#role: Portuguese commander and governor of India
afonso-de-albuquerque#summary: The Portuguese commander who conquered Goa, Malacca and Hormuz and established Portugal's maritime empire in Asia.
afonso-de-albuquerque#text: Albuquerque was governor of Portuguese India from 1509. He pursued the plan of controlling the main sea routes of the Indian Ocean through fortified bases: he conquered Goa in 1510, Malacca in 1511 and Hormuz on the Persian Gulf in 1515. In Malacca he had the fortress of A Famosa built and sent envoys to Siam and ships to the Moluccas. His warfare was often ruthless, for example towards the Muslim population of Goa. He died in 1515 on the voyage back to Goa, shortly after learning that he had been replaced.
miguel-lopez-de-legazpi#role: Spanish conqueror and first governor-general of the Philippines
miguel-lopez-de-legazpi#summary: The Spanish official and navigator who conquered the Philippines for Spain and founded Manila in 1571.
miguel-lopez-de-legazpi#text: Legazpi came from the Basque Country and lived for many years as an official in Mexico before King Philip II entrusted him with leading an expedition across the Pacific. In 1565 he landed on Cebu and founded the first permanent Spanish settlement in the islands. Through treaties, alliances and force he extended Spanish rule, and in 1571 he captured Maynila, where he founded the capital of the colony. As governor-general he laid the foundations of Spanish administration and of the galleon trade with Mexico. He died in Manila in 1572.
jan-pieterszoon-coen#role: Governor-general of the Dutch East India Company
jan-pieterszoon-coen#summary: The VOC governor-general who founded Batavia in 1619 and enforced the spice monopoly with great violence.
jan-pieterszoon-coen#text: Coen came from Hoorn in Holland and rose quickly in the VOC. As governor-general he captured Jayakarta in 1619 and founded Batavia as the company's headquarters in Asia. In 1621 he had the Banda Islands subjugated to enforce the monopoly on nutmeg; much of the native population was killed, enslaved or driven out, and enslaved people then worked the plantations. In the Netherlands he was long honoured as the founder of the colonial empire; today he is criticized for this violence. He died in Batavia in 1629 while the city was under siege by the Sultanate of Mataram.
stamford-raffles#role: British colonial official and founder of Singapore
stamford-raffles#summary: The British colonial official who governed Java and founded Singapore as a free port in 1819.
stamford-raffles#text: Raffles worked for the British East India Company and from 1811 to 1816 was governor of British-occupied Java. There he introduced land tax reforms, had Borobudur uncovered and wrote a history of Java. In 1819 he acquired the island of Singapore through a treaty with a prince of Johor and made it a free port, which quickly grew into one of the most important ports in Asia. He collected plants and animals and, after his return, founded the Zoological Society of London. He died in England in 1826.
gia-long#role: First emperor of the Nguyễn dynasty
gia-long#summary: The prince who united all of Vietnam in 1802 after decades of war against the Tây Sơn and founded the Nguyễn dynasty.
gia-long#text: Nguyễn Ánh was a member of the Nguyễn lords, whom the Tây Sơn had almost completely wiped out. He fled for a time to Siam and sought support in France through the French bishop Pigneau de Behaine; weapons and a few French officers helped him regain the south. In 1802 he conquered the north and took the name Gia Long as emperor. He ruled from Huế, reorganized administration and law on the Chinese model and had roads and fortresses built. Despite their help, he granted the French no special rights.
chulalongkorn#summary: The king of Siam who modernized his country and preserved it as the only state in Southeast Asia free of colonial rule.
chulalongkorn#text: Chulalongkorn came to the throne as a teenager in 1868 and reigned for more than 42 years. He abolished the obligation to prostrate oneself before the king, gradually ended slavery and corvée labour, and from 1892 created ministries on the European model. Under him schools, a modern army, a postal service, telegraphs and the first railways were established. In foreign policy he played the British and French off against each other and ceded outlying territories to save the heartland. He travelled to Europe in 1897 and 1907. In Thailand he is still revered as a great reformer.
jose-rizal#role: Writer, physician and national hero of the Philippines
jose-rizal#summary: The physician and writer whose novels denounced Spanish colonial rule and whose execution in 1896 fuelled the revolution.
jose-rizal#text: Rizal studied medicine and philosophy in Manila, Madrid and Heidelberg and spoke many languages. In Berlin he published the novel Noli Me Tángere in 1887, followed by El Filibusterismo in 1891; both depict the arbitrary rule of colonial officials and the abuse of power by the religious orders. He called for reforms and equal rights, not armed revolt. In 1892 he founded the Liga Filipina and was shortly afterwards exiled to Dapitan on Mindanao. After the revolution broke out he was put on trial and shot in Manila on 30 December 1896; the day is now a national holiday.
emilio-aguinaldo#role: Revolutionary leader and first president of the Philippines
emilio-aguinaldo#summary: The revolutionary leader who proclaimed the independence of the Philippines in 1898 and became the first president of the republic.
emilio-aguinaldo#text: Aguinaldo was a mayor in Cavite and in the revolution of 1896 became the most successful military leader of the Katipunan. He prevailed in the power struggle with Andrés Bonifacio, who was executed in 1897. After an agreement with Spain Aguinaldo went into exile in Hong Kong, returned in 1898 with American support and proclaimed independence at Kawit on 12 June. In 1899 he became president of the First Philippine Republic and led the war against the United States until he was captured in 1901. He died in Quezon City near Manila in 1964.
ansgar#summary: The Frankish monk who, as the “Apostle of the North”, undertook the first missionary journeys to Denmark and Sweden.
ansgar#text: Ansgar came from northern France and was educated at the monasteries of Corbie and Corvey. Around 826 he accompanied the baptized Danish king Harald Klak to the North, and around 830 he preached in Birka. In 831 he became the first archbishop of Hamburg; after Vikings destroyed it in 845 he led the mission from Bremen and founded churches in Hedeby and Ribe. Lasting success eluded him, but the Church venerates him as a saint and patron of Scandinavia.
alfred-der-grosse#summary: The Anglo-Saxon king who alone held out against the Vikings and laid the foundations for a united England.
alfred-der-grosse#text: Alfred became king of Wessex in 871, in the middle of the war against the Great Heathen Army. After a defeat early in 878 he gathered new forces from Athelney and defeated Guthrum at Edington. He then had a network of fortified places, the burhs, built, improved the levy and built ships. He promoted learning, had Latin works translated into Old English, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle probably originated at his court. He is the only Anglo-Saxon king to bear the epithet “the Great”.
rollo#role: Viking leader and first ruler of Normandy
rollo#summary: The Viking to whom the West Frankish king ceded the land on the lower Seine in 911, thereby founding Normandy.
rollo#text: The sources disagree on Rollo’s origins: Norman chroniclers make him a Dane, Icelandic sagas identify him with the Norwegian Gange-Hrolf. What is certain is that around 900 he led a Viking band on the Seine and in 911 came to terms with Charles the Simple. He was baptized, took the name Robert and ruled from Rouen; only his successors bore the title of duke. He died around 930. His descendant in the fifth generation was William the Conqueror.
harald-blauzahn#summary: The Danish king who was baptized around 965 and boasted on the Jelling runestone that he had united Denmark and made the Danes Christian.
harald-blauzahn#text: Harald, son of Gorm the Old, reigned from about 958 until around 986. He had the burial complex at Jelling enlarged and the great runestone erected there; under him the ring fortresses such as Trelleborg and Fyrkat and the bridge at Ravning Enge were also built. For a time he also ruled parts of Norway. Around 986 a revolt by his son Sweyn Forkbeard drove him out, and he died shortly afterwards. The wireless technology Bluetooth is named after him, and its logo combines his initials in runes.
erik-der-rote#role: Explorer and founder of the Greenland settlements
erik-der-rote#summary: The Norwegian-born seafarer, banished from Iceland, who founded the Norse settlement of Greenland around 985.
erik-der-rote#text: Erik Thorvaldsson, called “the Red” after his red hair, came to Iceland as a child with his father after the latter had been banished from Norway for killings. Erik too was outlawed for killings and used his three years of banishment to explore Greenland. Around 985 he led settlers there and made his home at the farm of Brattahlíð in the south, where he lived as the most respected man of the colony. According to the sagas he remained true to the old faith, unlike his wife Thjodhild.
leif-eriksson#summary: The son of Erik the Red who around 1000 became one of the first Europeans to reach the coast of North America.
leif-eriksson#text: Leif grew up in Iceland and Greenland. According to Erik the Red’s Saga he was baptized in Norway at the court of Olaf Tryggvason and was to bring Christianity to Greenland. Around 1000 he sailed west, sighted Helluland and Markland and wintered in Vinland, which he is said to have named after the grapes found there. The two sagas describe his voyage differently, and much remains uncertain. After his return he took over his father’s farm at Brattahlíð; in the United States Leif Erikson Day is observed on 9 October.
gudrid-thorbjarnardottir#summary: The Icelandic woman who according to the sagas settled in Vinland with Thorfinn Karlsefni and gave birth to a son there.
gudrid-thorbjarnardottir#text: Gudrid lived around the year 1000 and is known only from the Vinland sagas. She came from Iceland to Greenland, married Thorfinn Karlsefni after the death of her first husband and accompanied him on his attempt at settlement in Vinland. There her son Snorri was born, according to tradition the first child of European parents in America. She later lived in Iceland and as a widow is said to have made a pilgrimage to Rome. She is regarded as one of the most widely travelled women of her time, but many details of her life are uncertain.
olav-tryggvason#summary: The Norwegian king who tried to impose Christianity by force and died around 1000 in the naval battle of Svolder.
olav-tryggvason#text: According to tradition Olaf grew up in exile, among other places in Kievan Rus, and in the 990s led Viking raids on England, where he was baptized. In 995 he returned to Norway and became king. In his short reign he forced chieftains and farmers to be baptized, destroyed sanctuaries and put pressure on Iceland, Greenland, the Faroes and Orkney. Around 1000 he was defeated by his enemies at Svolder. The later sagas made him a hero, but the accounts of his youth are largely legendary.
knut-der-grosse#role: King of England, Denmark and Norway
knut-der-grosse#summary: The Danish king who united England, Denmark and Norway in a North Sea Empire.
knut-der-grosse#text: Cnut, son of Sweyn Forkbeard, conquered England in 1016 and ruled it for almost twenty years in peace with Anglo-Saxon and Danish magnates. He inherited Denmark around 1018 and won Norway in 1028. As a Christian king he promoted the Church, made gifts to monasteries and in 1027 travelled to Rome for the imperial coronation of Conrad II. The well-known story that he commanded the waves to retreat dates only from the 12th century. After his death in 1035 his empire fell apart under his sons.
olav-der-heilige#role: King of Norway and the country’s patron saint
olav-der-heilige#summary: The Norwegian king Olaf Haraldsson, who fell at Stiklestad in 1030 and as a saint became “Norway’s eternal king”.
olav-der-heilige#text: As a young man Olaf Haraldsson went on Viking expeditions to England and France and was probably baptized in Normandy. In 1015 he returned to Norway, became king and imposed Christianity with church laws and a firm hand. In 1028 he had to flee from Cnut the Great and fell at Stiklestad on his return in 1030. Soon miracles at his tomb in Nidaros were seen as proof of his sanctity. His cult contributed significantly to Norway becoming a Christian kingdom.
harald-hardrada#summary: The Norwegian king Harald Sigurdsson, called “the Hard Ruler”, who served in Byzantium and fell at Stamford Bridge in 1066.
harald-hardrada#text: As a youth Harald fought at Stiklestad in 1030 beside his half-brother Olaf and then fled to Kievan Rus. Later he served in the Byzantine emperor’s Varangian Guard and fought in Sicily and Bulgaria, among other places. He returned around 1045 with great wealth, became co-king in 1046 and from 1047 sole ruler of Norway. For years he waged war against Denmark. In 1066 he claimed England and fell at Stamford Bridge; his death is regarded as the end of the Viking Age.
snorri-sturluson#summary: The author of the Prose Edda and Heimskringla, the most important historian of the medieval North.
snorri-sturluson#text: Snorri came from the powerful Sturlung family, grew up at the centre of learning at Oddi and became one of the richest men in Iceland; twice he was lawspeaker of the Althing. Around 1220 he wrote the Prose Edda and around 1230 Heimskringla, a history of the Norwegian kings from their legendary beginnings to 1177; Egil’s Saga is also often attributed to him. Entangled in the power struggles between the Icelandic families and the Norwegian king, he was killed in 1241 at his farm of Reykholt, probably with the approval of King Haakon IV.
waldemar-iv-atterdag#summary: The Danish king who restored his fragmented realm, conquered Visby and was defeated in the war against the Hanseatic League.
waldemar-iv-atterdag#text: When Valdemar became king in 1340, Denmark was almost entirely pledged to the counts of Holstein. Step by step he bought and conquered the land back, selling Estonia to the Teutonic Order in 1346 to do so, and recovered Scania from Sweden in 1360. In 1361 he conquered Gotland and Visby, which led to war with the Hanseatic League, which forced him into the Peace of Stralsund in 1370. His epithet Atterdag probably means “another day”. His daughter Margaret became the dominant ruler of the North after his death in 1375.
margarete-i#role: Queen and regent of Denmark, Norway and Sweden
margarete-i#summary: The Danish king’s daughter who brought all three Nordic realms under her rule and founded the Kalmar Union in 1397.
margarete-i#text: Margaret, daughter of Valdemar IV, was married at the age of ten to King Haakon VI of Norway. After her father’s death she secured the Danish throne in 1376 for her son Olaf, who also inherited Norway in 1380. When Olaf died in 1387, she had herself recognized as ruler in both realms, defeated King Albert of Sweden in 1389 and thus governed the entire North. In 1397 she had her great-nephew Eric of Pomerania crowned at Kalmar, but kept power until her death in Flensburg in 1412. She is buried in Roskilde Cathedral.
franz-von-assisi#role: Founder of an order and saint
franz-von-assisi#summary: The merchant’s son from Assisi who renounced his possessions, lived in poverty and founded the Franciscan order.
franz-von-assisi#text: Francis, born in 1181 or 1182 as the son of a wealthy cloth merchant, turned away from his former life after war, captivity and illness and publicly renounced his father. He preached penance, poverty and peace and gathered companions from whom the Order of Friars Minor emerged; with Clare of Assisi a women’s order came into being. In 1219, during the Fifth Crusade, he travelled to Egypt and met Sultan al-Kamil there. His “Canticle of the Sun” is regarded as one of the first poems in the Italian language. He died in 1226 and was canonized as early as 1228.
jan-hus#role: Theologian and church reformer in Prague
jan-hus#summary: The Bohemian preacher who denounced abuses in the Church and was burned as a heretic at the Council of Constance in 1415.
jan-hus#text: Hus was born around 1370 in Husinec in southern Bohemia, taught at the University of Prague and from 1402 preached in Czech at the Bethlehem Chapel. Influenced by the writings of the Englishman John Wycliffe, he criticized the wealth of the Church and the sale of indulgences and placed the Bible above the authority of the pope. In 1414 he travelled to Constance with a safe conduct from King Sigismund, but was arrested there and, because he would not recant, burned on 6 July 1415. In the Czech Republic he is regarded as a national hero; his teachings influenced the Reformation of the 16th century.
